options: An approach that treats an incident as a system failure to understand and fix, rather than a person to punish
A postmortem written without any documentation of what happened
A postmortem that only management is allowed to read
A postmortem that assigns responsibility to a single named individual
questions.explain: Blameless postmortems focus on the system and process gaps that allowed an incident, since blame discourages honesty in future reports.

questions.q: Why does assigning blame in a postmortem work against learning, per this lesson?
options: It teaches people to hide mistakes and omit details in future incidents
It has no real effect on future reporting honesty
It automatically fixes the underlying technical issue
SQL Server logs prevent blame from being assigned
questions.explain: When people fear punishment, they become less forthcoming about what actually happened, undermining the postmortem's purpose.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend for building an incident timeline?
options: Pulling timestamped, factual events from real sources like alert logs and session data, rather than reconstructing from memory afterward
Writing a narrative essay based on general recollection after the incident is resolved
Skipping the timeline entirely and focusing only on the fix
Using only the on-call DBA's personal notes taken after the fact
questions.explain: Memory compresses and reorders events under stress, so the timeline should be built from actual timestamped sources.

questions.q: What is the difference between a root cause and a contributing factor, as this lesson describes it?
options: The root cause is the underlying trigger; a contributing factor is a condition that worsened the incident or delayed detection alongside it
There is no meaningful difference — they are the same thing
A contributing factor is always more important than the root cause
Root causes only apply to hardware failures
questions.explain: Both deserve documentation — fixing contributing factors (like a missing alert) can prevent a repeat as effectively as fixing the root cause.

questions.q: What makes an action item strong, per this lesson's test?
options: It is specific, assigned, and structural — such that if it had existed before, the incident wouldn't have happened or would have been caught faster
It is vague enough to apply to any future incident
It assigns blame to whoever was on call during the incident
It requires no owner and no specific change to any process
questions.explain: A good action item changes something structural (an alert, a checklist step, a runbook entry) rather than issuing a vague call for more care.
